Q: How to run jq from gitbash in Windows? A:

You may deal with that in PowerShell even when there's no jq because it has built-in support for various structured text formats like JSON, XML, CSV... The file can be parsed directly into .NET objects that you can manipulate easily. For this purpose you can use ConvertFrom-Json and ConvertTo-Json

# Open the json file and modify the properties
$config = Get-Content -Path "config.json" | ConvertFrom-Json
$config.AppSettings.LogLevel = "Info"
$config.ServiceSettings.MaxUsers = 200

# Convert the modified object back and save it:
$config | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 3 | Set-Content -Path "config.json"

See also

  • PowerShell : retrieve JSON object by field value
  • Playing with JSON and PowerShell
  • Working with JSON data in PowerShell
  • PowerShell and JSON: A Practical Guide
  • Parsing JSON with PowerShell

Q: Is there a way to speed up signtool? It is slow A:

Use Sign (part of .Net Foundation). Final version has not been released yet but it works very well.

Sign can be used to sign files with the following certificate sources:

  • Local certificate file

  • Windows Certificate Store

  • Azure Key Vault

  • Azure Artifact Signing

It is available via NuGet and you can install with the following dotnet command (--prerelease is necessary until final version be released):

dotnet tool install -g --prerelease sign

After installing you can view help typing the following command:

sign code --help

Q: What is the proper WCAG markup for radio buttons with comboboxes A:

Drop `role="radiogroup"` entirely. That's what the checkers are objecting to, and
you don't need it.

`radiogroup` has required owned elements in the ARIA spec: only `radio`. A
combobox inside it breaks that, and it's not pedantry, AT works out "radio 2 of
3" from the owned radios, so unexpected children make that unreliable.

But native radios sharing a `name` are already a radio group. The browser
exposes the grouping, the set size and the position with no ARIA at all. So
`fieldset` + `legend` isn't a workaround, it's just the right markup, and the
legend names the group, which is what people are usually after when they put
`aria-label` on a radiogroup.

Arrow keys come from the shared `name`, not from the role, so removing the role
doesn't remove them. If they stopped working, check that the radios still share
a name, that nothing is calling `preventDefault()` on keydown, and that you
haven't left `role="radio"` on the inputs. That last one overrides the native
role and you inherit responsibility for all the keyboard handling yourself.

The thing I'd actually worry about in your markup isn't the grouping though,
it's this:

r.parentNode.nextElementSibling.disabled = r != event.target

You're right that it isn't announced, and that's a 4.1.2 problem. Someone using
a screen reader picks a radio and gets told nothing about the fields that just
became available.

You can bolt a polite live region onto it ("Date range enabled") but I'd change
the approach instead: don't disable, just render the fieldset that belongs to
the selected radio and drop the other one. Then there's nothing to announce,
because nothing announced is inoperable. Disabled fields are skipped in the tab
order anyway and people navigating by form control routinely never find out
they exist.

Side note on

\[disabled\] { filter: grayscale(100%) opacity(.4); }

at 0.4 opacity your labels are well under 4.5:1. Technically fine, 1.4.3 excepts
"text that is part of an inactive user interface component", but if a sighted
user can't read the label of a field they're being asked to choose between,
you've satisfied the criterion and not the user. Another reason to show/hide
rather than enable/disable.

If those comboboxes are custom widgets rather than `select`, they've got their
own structure to get right (`role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`,
focus management) and that's a separate problem from this one.

Q: Git - creating a pretty log using rebase A:

2026: There is still no rebase option that makes rewriting a branch shared by several developers safe.

However, newer Git versions provide much better ways to separate:

  • the real collaborative history used by developers
  • the simplified integration history wanted by the release team
  • the ability to check exactly what each user story added

Git 2.19: compare a branch before and after rebasing

Git 2.19 (Sept. 2018) introduced git range-diff, which compares two versions of the same commit series.

I feel that as rebase loses information about the order in which commits really happened

I did mention in August 2018 comparing changes across a rebase, meaning that, after a rebase, you can use:

git range-diff @{u} @{1} @

It associates the original commits with their rewritten equivalents and highlights commits that were added, removed, reordered, or modified.

For the OP, it makes it easier to check that rebasing a temporary copy of the feature branch did not change or lose any part of the user story. It does not make rebasing the shared feature branch safe.

Git 2.36: inspect what conflict resolution added

Git 2.36 (Apr. 2022) introduced --remerge-diff:

git show --remerge-diff <merge-commit>

if they need to sync the branch code with some changes pushed to master, they cannot

I have previously, in February 2022, mentioned how --remerge-diff can inspect a past merge resolution: Git recreates the mechanical merge and compares it with the result actually committed.

For the OP, developers could synchronize a shared feature branch by merging master into it instead of rebasing it. If that merge has conflicts, --remerge-diff makes their manual resolutions easier to review.

Git 2.38: update related local branches

Git 2.38 (Oct. 2022) introduced git rebase --update-refs.

It works well most of the time, but when more than a single developer work on the same branch, they cannot rebase with master.

I described, in August 2022, how --update-refs automatically moves local branches pointing to commits being rebased:

git rebase --update-refs origin/master

For the OP, it can help when a developer has other local branches pointing into the history being rebased.

But it does not update branches in other developers' clones, so --update-refs does not solve the OP's main problem: a published branch used by several developers should still not normally be rebased.

Git 2.43: show exactly what each merge introduced

Git 2.43 (Nov. 2023) introduced --dd, a shorthand for showing merge diffs against the first parent:

git log master --first-parent --merges --dd

They say that it will allow them to see and control what goes to production.

I explained before, in August 2020, how a first-parent diff shows the changes introduced by a merge. --dd provides a shorter way to request that view.

For the OP, this shows the complete change each user-story merge added to master, without hiding or rewriting the detailed development history.

Practical solution

I would keep the shared development branch intact and allow its developers to synchronize it normally:

git fetch origin
git switch story-123
git merge origin/master
git push origin story-123

That preserves the actual collaboration history and does not require every other developer to recover from a forced update.

When the story is ready, create a disposable branch from master:

git fetch origin

git switch -c story-123-integration origin/master
git merge --squash origin/story-123

The staged result can be reviewed before it is committed:

git diff --cached

Then create one commit representing the story and merge that temporary branch with --no-ff:

git commit -m "Story 123"                 # Squashed commit 'Q' of story-123

git switch master
git merge --no-ff story-123-integration

The resulting integration history has one merge commit on master and one simple story commit on its temporary branch:

                 C---D---S---E     story-123
                /       /
---A---B-------+-------+------M--- master
        \                    /
         Q-------------------      story-123-integration

The complete collaborative history still exists on story-123, including its individual commits and synchronization merges, provided that branch, or another archival ref pointing to it, is retained.

The release team can use:

git log master --first-parent --merges --oneline --decorate

to obtain the clean story-oriented history, and:

git show --dd <merge-commit>                       # M in previous diagram

to see exactly what a particular story introduced into production.

When a synchronization merge on the original feature branch involved conflict resolution, it can be inspected with:

git show --remerge-diff <synchronization-merge>    # S in previous diagram

If the team prefers to preserve the feature's individual commits in the final integration, instead of reducing the story to one commit with merge --squash, it can rebase a temporary copy of the feature branch onto the current master.

          C---D-------S---E                   story-123
         /           /
A---B---X-----------Y--------------------M--- master
                     \                  /
                      C'---D'---E'------      story-123-integration
  • C-D-S-E is the original shared feature history
  • S is a synchronization merge bringing newer master changes into story-123
  • story-123 is left untouched
  • C'-D'-E' are the individual feature commits replayed onto the current master (Y)
  • M is the final --no-ff merge of that temporary branch into master

Before creating M, git range-diff can compare the original commit series with C'-D'-E' and help check that the rebase did not unexpectedly change or lose part of the story.

The original story-123 history is still useful: it records how the feature was actually developed, keeps the original commit IDs, and preserves synchronization merge S. If S required manual conflict resolution, it can still be inspected with:

git show --remerge-diff S

It can be important because a normal rebase does not preserve the synchronization merge itself, and changes made specifically while resolving that merge deserve separate review.

The two histories serve different purposes:

  • story-123 preserves the real collaborative history, while
  • story-123-integration provides the cleaner history that will become visible through master.

Whether the temporary copy is squashed into one story commit or rebased to preserve its individual commits, the important point is that the shared feature branch itself is not rewritten.

That gives both developers and the release team what they need:

  • developers can collaborate and synchronize with master normally
  • the original development history remains available on story-123
  • master has one visible merge per user story
  • the rebased alternative can preserve individual feature commits if you want to
  • range-diff can check the rewritten commit series before integration
  • --first-parent provides the requested release view
  • --dd shows exactly what each story added
  • --remerge-diff shows changes made while resolving synchronization merges

The clean log should be treated as an integration view, not as a reason to rewrite the history on which several developers are actively collaborating.
